title: A conversation
hookLine: a sacred hadith says Allah answers each line of the Fatiha as it is said (Muslim)

lines: WHAT IF EVERY LINE GOT A REPLY?
cards: There's a kind of phone call where you talk and nobody answers. Voicemail. You say your piece into the quiet, hang up, and hope it lands.
Prayer can sound like that from the outside: words going out, silence coming back. Sahih Muslim preserves a hadith that pictures the Fatiha very differently.
In it, every line the worshipper says gets a reply, right then, before the next line starts. Not voicemail. Today: a conversation.

teach.h: A SACRED HADITH, IN SAHIH MUSLIM
teach.b: This is a hadith qudsi, a sacred hadith: words the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ reported from God Himself, but which are not part of the Qur'an.

God says: I have divided the prayer between Myself and My servant into two halves, and My servant will have what he asks. Then it walks through the surah. The servant says: praise be to Allah, Lord of the Worlds.
And God says: My servant has praised Me. The Beneficent, the Merciful: My servant has extolled Me. Owner of the Day of Judgment: My servant has glorified Me.
Then the hinge, the middle verse: Thee alone we worship, Thee alone we ask for help. And God says: this is between Me and My servant, and My servant will have what he asked.
Then the last lines, show us the straight path, and God says: this is for My servant, and My servant will have what he asked. Notice the shape. The first half belongs to God: praise.
The middle is shared. The last half belongs to the person: a request. And every line gets an answer.
One detail stands out: the replies aren't promised for a perfect recitation; they're described as coming each time the line is said.
That's why some teachers tell people to pause a breath after each verse. Not because the reply needs time. Because the one praying needs a moment to remember there is one.

how: Many Muslims recite al-Fatiha slowly, pausing at the end of each verse; teachers often cite the hadith qudsi in Sahih Muslim, in which God answers each line, as the reason for the pause.

games.q: who answers what — tap the pairs.
p: praise be to Allah, Lord of the Worlds

s: a hadith qudsi is a verse of the Qur'an

in the hadith, God answers every line of the Fatiha
Sahih Muslim walks through the surah line by line.

games.q: you reach the middle verse: Thee alone we worship, Thee alone we ask for help. in the hadith, whose verse is it?
o: shared between God and the servant.
games.why: shared: this is between Me and My servant. worship faces God, asking for help faces the person, and the verse holds both.

practice: Say the Fatiha now, aloud or silently, in Arabic or in English, and stop for one breath after each verse. In that breath, recall the reply from the hadith: praised, extolled, glorified, between Me and My servant, for My servant.
If you don't pray, simply listen to the gaps between the lines, and to how the words feel with space around them.
